17511: I'll go get rid of the evil thing
17512: As a child they traveled with their family's escort business. At sixteen they met bandits on a mountain road and walked for three days alone guarding the wounded before finding a village. Since then they always check the way out before making a move. In idle hours they like polishing an old saber and listening to merchants' tales of faraway places. When traveling with others they never rush anyone, but always count heads when the group regathers.
17513: Born in a remote mountain village, they learned to recognize plants from herb gatherers as a child. Once, searching for a missing companion in a rainstorm, they were trapped in the deep mountains for two nights and survived on wild fruit and spring water. They still love collecting rare herbs, can't help lending a hand when they see someone hurt, and always carry a few packets of common medicinal powder.
17514: In their early years they were a porter at a river port, used to all kinds of ships and jianghu travelers. They once dived into rapids to save a drowning child and were left with an old ache in the shoulders and back on rainy days. They like sitting on the bank watching the water, are good at making a pot of hot soup from cheap ingredients, and when people argue, they usually get them to sit down and eat first.
17515: They grew up in an opera troupe, learning somersaults, spear dancing and a few lines of song, but never got to play the lead. After the troupe broke up they set out alone and worked their stage moves into their martial arts. They still love busy markets, always stop to listen to opera until the end, and sometimes paint simple opera masks on children's faces.
17516: Their family made porcelain for generations, until a kiln fire cost them the shop in their youth and they left home with only half an unfired teacup. Later they learned martial arts to make a living, but they still work with the patience of shaping clay. They love plain tea and quiet, often mend broken things so the cracks can't be seen, and can't stand being rushed or pressured in conversation.
17517: As a youngster they herded the village's horses and grew unusually alert to mountain paths and changes in the weather. One snowy night they led a frightened herd around a cliff edge and saved most of the village's livelihood. Since then they'll look after animals wherever they go, whittle wooden whistles in idle hours to play country tunes whose names they've forgotten, and often warn companions to take cover from rain by reading the wind.
17518: They were once an apprentice at a small-town apothecary, until the owner threw them out for secretly giving medicine on credit to poor families. They left with only an old medical book full of handwritten notes and treat minor ailments as they travel. They like sunbathing and tidying their medicine chest, hate it when anyone mocks the weak for being sick or hurt, and when thanked, only say to remember to help others later.
17519: As a child they lost everything in a flood and wandered from place to place with the refugees, once surviving hunger on a piece of dry ration a stranger shared. Having learned martial arts, they often give their own rations to those who need them more. They're not fussy about food or clothes but treasure rice and flour, frown at anyone wasting food, and carefully wrap up leftover rations after every meal.
17520: In their early years they copied books at an academy and learned plenty of characters, but couldn't afford the tuition and could only listen to lessons through the window. Later they worked out a few self-defense moves on their own from a tattered fist manual. They like collecting old books and stele inscriptions, jot down lines they don't understand on scraps of paper in their sleeve to puzzle over, and gladly write letters home for those who can't write.
17521: They once crossed the desert with a caravan. When sandstorms buried the road, they found water for everyone by reading the stars at night. That trip left them with the habit of always carrying water and never making promises lightly. In idle hours they like stargazing and drawing routes, leave a small mark wherever they've been, and fill in what they've seen in the margins of their map when they're not on the road.
17522: Born at a seaside salt works, they learned to read the tides and judge the drying of salt from an early age. As a youngster they risked crossing the flats at rising tide to fetch a doctor for a sick fellow worker. They still watch the sky in everything they do, like collecting oddly shaped shells and never complain however plain the food, but can't stand people looking down on those from laboring backgrounds.
17523: Their father was a village carpenter, and as a child they often steadied timber and handed planes for him. Once, when a roof beam collapsed, they worked out where people were trapped by sound alone and led a rescue through a side wall that saved a family of three. Since then they always carry a length of chalk line, love carving little animals in their free time, and never put off a repair they've promised.
17524: As a child they lived in the mountain forests with hunters but never liked needless killing. One hard winter they found an injured fawn and nursed it in secret until spring before letting it go. Later they learned to read who was coming from their tracks, yet rarely pry into others' secrets. They like roasting chestnuts and always share the catch with the old and frail first.
17525: They spent years as a handyman at a post station and know every well and rest shed on the official road. When a blizzard closed the roads, they led a horse out alone to deliver an urgent letter and lost the use of two fingers to frostbite. They treasure gloves and hot soup, turn their head without thinking at the sound of horse bells, and always remember travelers they've met only once.
17526: From a lakeside fishing village, they're an excellent swimmer, yet a capsizing in childhood left them in awe of the wind and waves at night. They once rowed a small boat all night searching for a missing fishing family and brought them back to shore by the light of one faint lamp. They like mending nets and drying small fish. They seem quiet, but when real danger comes they're the first to step forward.
17527: As a youngster they worked the bellows in a smithy and could tell good iron from bad by the sound of the hammer. When bandits raided the shop, they protected their master and the account books with a red-hot pair of tongs. In martial training they still polish every move over and over, like listening to rain on the roof tiles, and keep their weapons clean and well kept.
17528: They grew up on a mountain tea plantation and know picking, withering and roasting inside out. When a wildfire bore down on the village, they led everyone in cutting a firebreak and saved most of the tea bushes. They prefer quiet mornings alone, never care whether tea is expensive, only about the water temperature and aroma, and when they're upset they slowly sort tea leaves.
17529: They once kept accounts for a small trading house, lightning-fast on the abacus, until they were dismissed for refusing to cook the books for their employer. Before leaving, they helped the unpaid workers work out their wages one by one. Since then they've been especially sharp with numbers and always check their change. They like solving puzzles in idle hours and will always go the extra mile for honest, trustworthy people.
17530: As a child they lived with an old tomb keeper and grew used to partings and death, quieter than others their age. When a flash flood wrecked the cemetery, they found every scattered tombstone in the rain and put it back. They like sweeping quietly and tidying old things, never make jokes about the dead, and every Qingming they lay a bunch of wildflowers on the graves no one tends.
17531: Their family made lanterns for a living, and they're best at pasting paper and mixing warm-colored lamp oil. On the Lantern Festival night they knocked on door after door in a burning street and led the residents out through the back lanes. Since then they always take a second look at any open flame. They like collecting colored paper and are happy to leave a small lamp burning for children afraid of the dark.
17532: In their early years they guarded a salt merchant and traveled many remote trade routes. Once a companion embezzled silver and framed someone else; they uncovered the truth from the receipts along the way, and lost an old friend over it. Since then they're very careful about making friends, yet remember a single kindness for a long time. Their favorite thing is soaking their feet and listening to the wind at the end of a day's journey.
17533: They grew up in an escort agency but were never good with a saber, so they kept the routes and cargo lists instead. When bandits ambushed a shipment, they led the team to safety through an abandoned mine tunnel from memory. Since then they always check their pack over and over before setting out. They like drawing road signs, are very patient with people who get lost, and never laugh at anyone's poor sense of direction.
17534: After an earthquake destroyed every house in their hometown, they spent months with the craftsmen putting up shelters and repairing walls. In those days they learned to share out timber and calm frightened people. Now when they see a loose beam or pillar they shore it up unasked. They like sturdy, durable things rather than flashy ones and rarely waste a single nail.
17535: As a youngster they pushed carts in a mine and grew very alert to underground echoes and cracks in the rock. Once they heard an odd sound before a cave-in and stopped the work in time, saving dozens of lives. Though they left the mine, they still dislike cramped, dark places. In idle hours they like sunbathing and grinding stones, and always remind companions not to show off by taking risks.
17536: They once worked in a weaving workshop and can tell whether cloth will last from how tight the warp and weft are. When floodwater soaked the workshop, they led the other women in moving the silk and account books overnight. Their fingers are still nimble; they like sewing hidden pockets and mending hems, and when they see someone's clothes torn they often quietly hand them a needle and thread.
17537: As a child they traveled the rivers with a ship's doctor and know a bit about treating seasickness, wounds and unfamiliar climates. When an epidemic spread through the fleet, they insisted on keeping the sick separate from the drinking water and saved many passengers. They always carry dried ginger and a water-filter cloth, love the smell of medicine, and hate the smell of liquor in a closed cabin.
17538: They once assisted a vet at a horse market and are good at calming frightened animals. They spotted a disease from a warhorse's unusual breathing and stopped it spreading through the whole stud. They speak softly and slowly, like grooming animals, and won't hesitate to step in against anyone who drives animals roughly.
17539: In their youth they cooked in an army camp and saw many soldiers revived by a bowl of hot porridge. When a grain cart got stuck in the mud during a retreat, they had it taken apart and the grain shared out, making sure the wounded ate first. Now they cook enough with nothing left over, like experimenting with pickles, and always ask new companions if there's anything they don't eat.
17540: They were once a young constable at the county yamen, until they quit rather than torture a confession out of anyone. Before leaving, they spent months on the case and found the real thief for a wrongly accused porter. They still habitually look at the mud on people's soles and the way they talk, like patrolling the streets in the early morning, and find bullying especially hard to tolerate.
17541: They grew up with a spice caravan and can tell dozens of fragrant woods and seeds apart. When rain soaked the warehouse, they saved most of the goods by re-drying and re-blending them. A faint fragrance always clings to their pockets. They like spicy food and foreign tales, and when they catch an unfamiliar scent they can't help tracking down where it comes from.
17542: Born by a frozen river in the north, they often cut ice to fetch water for the villagers in winter. Once they heard the ice rumble and stopped a train of carts from crossing just in time; moments later the river cracked apart. They still test their footing before every step and love thick boots and hot wine, but don't like people exaggerating and bragging about how they survived the cold.
17543: Their family has woven bamboo goods for generations, and they learned to split strips, weave baskets and mend umbrella ribs as a child. When the mountain village ran short of grain, they led the villagers in building a temporary rope bridge of bamboo to carry food across. They can't keep their hands still, tying little knots even while waiting. They love the sound of wind in bamboo and have little patience for people who give up halfway.
17544: As a youngster they traveled with a storyteller, performing everywhere and hearing countless heroic tales. When the storyteller fell ill, they held the stage alone for half a month, trading stories for medicine money. They're a fine talker now but won't paint themselves as a hero. They like collecting folk ghost stories and adjust what they say by reading their listeners' faces.
17545: As a child they lived at a temple, sweeping the bell tower and topping up the lamp oil. When lightning wrecked the gate in a storm, they rang the bell to gather the monks and rescue trapped pilgrims. They later left the temple to travel but still rise at dawn, love long, lingering echoes, and when their mind is in turmoil they count their breaths over and over to calm down.
17546: They once tended hives for a beekeeper and learned to move colonies with the flowering seasons. After a wildfire scattered the bees, it took a whole season to gather them again. They love sweets but won't let themselves eat much, carry ointment for insect stings, and believe flailing in a panic only makes things worse.
17547: Born in a salt-well town, as a youngster they turned the windlass and recorded the length of the well rope. Once, when water seeped through the well wall, they risked going down to secure the rope, buying the workers time to escape. Since then they don't like standing at the edge of deep wells, tie every knot perfectly, and never pretend not to hear a companion's cry for help.
17548: In their early years they rafted timber through the river gorges and learned to read currents and avoid hidden rocks. When a flood crest came, they cut loose their own family's raft so the logs would block a breach and protect the villages downstream. They still run a hand over good timber, love the sound of waves, and though they seem slow to decide, they rarely regret a choice.
17549: They once worked as a night watchman at the city granary and know the smell of damp and weevil-eaten grain. One year before a famine they noticed irregular accounts and reported it overnight, saving stores that were being sold off on the sly. They have deep respect for farmers, never leave a grain of rice uneaten, like drying grain in their free time, and carefully check every sack of rations.
17550: Their mother ran a small tailor's shop, and they learned to measure and cut cloth as a child. They once remade old clothes into fitted winter wear for a group of refugee children and missed the convoy out of the city because of it. Later, in martial training, they still put freedom of movement first, like experimenting with pockets and straps, and can't help admiring finely stitched clothes.
17551: As a youngster they worked at a paper mill, scooping pulp and drying sheets, their hands often wrinkled white from the cold water. Once a spark fell into the paper store; they smelled it before the smoke rose and moved the oil away in time. They treasure every sheet of paper and cut up miswritten pages into notes. They like pressing leaves between pages and can't stand people who tear books roughly.
17552: They once worked at a village winery and know steaming grain, sealing jars and telling when wine has gone bad. After their master died, they guarded the cellar alone until every unpaid worker got their wages, and only then left. They can hold their drink but rarely overindulge, love the smell of new wine, and when someone uses drink as an excuse to cause trouble, they take the bowl away at once.
17553: From a quarrying village, as a youngster they carved thresholds and well rims with a chisel for a living. When rocks fell from a cliff, they judged where they'd roll and led their fellow workers to shelter in an abandoned stone trough. Since then they're always alert to what's overhead. They like feeling the grain of different stones, are steady in their work, and once they set a goal they chip away at it until it's done.
17554: They served tea at a go parlor for years and picked up a few opening strategies along the way. When a local strongman set up a swindle, they replayed the game and showed how he'd switched the stones. They like to think three moves ahead, collect old go stones and don't care about winning or losing; they only hate it when people use seniority to bully beginners.
17555: As a child they traveled the villages with a folk musician and can play the flute and mend strings. When a plague sealed the village, they stayed at the village gate playing so the people in quarantine could hear familiar tunes every day. They like recording local songs, tap out a soft beat when they're in a good mood, and feel especially close to anyone willing to listen quietly to a whole tune.
17556: They once chopped vegetables and tended the fires in a big inn's kitchen, able to watch three woks at once at the busiest times. The night the kitchen caught fire, they shut the oil vats first and then woke the guests, leaving a burn scar on their arm. They like working out portable meals, go on alert at any smell of burning, and always save the first hot bowl for whoever comes back last.
17557: As a youngster they helped build a stone bridge across a valley, hauling sand and aligning the piers. When floodwater hit the scaffolding, they tied a rope around themselves and went into the water to save a craftsman who'd fallen in. They still check for cracks every time they cross a bridge, love sturdy ropes and stone arches, and hold a special respect for unremarkable things that bear the load.
17558: Their hometown watered its fields with waterwheels, and they learned to fix gears and clear channels as a child. In a year of great drought they guarded the channel mouth night after night to stop powerful families upstream from taking all the water. The sound of running water puts them at ease. They like tinkering with small mechanisms and insist that everyone takes their turn with the water by the rules.
17559: They once raised eaglets for a frontier falconer and learned to earn trust through patience. In a sandstorm they released a hawk to search for a lost party and found three children by following its cries. They love high places and open skies, hate snares that bind too tight, and never force anyone to obey at once.
17560: In their early years they were a rural postal runner, walking every village and town nearby with a mailbag. When the river bridge collapsed, they took a hundred-li detour just to hand a family the news of a fallen soldier in person. They take every letter seriously, like collecting seals from different places, and always deliver a promised message word for word.
17561: They learned to fix wheels, grease axles and tend mules at a cart company. When an axle broke on a long-distance convoy, they took apart their own cart bed to make a temporary brace so the wounded could reach the city in time. They always check wheels and soles before setting out, love the sound of a wooden wheel turning smoothly, and rarely mind a long road.
17562: They grew up in a stockade on the northern frontier and gathered firewood under the beacon towers as a child. Once a false alarm nearly caused chaos; they climbed the tower in the snow and found it was only dust kicked up by a herd. Since then they insist on seeing things with their own eyes. They love broad horizons and strong tea, and especially dislike news that spreads before it's checked.
17563: Their family ran an umbrella shop, and they can tell oiled paper, bamboo ribs and different kinds of rain apart. When a rainstorm washed away a street bridge, they lashed bundles of umbrella ribs into a float to save people. On cloudy days they remind companions to bring umbrellas, love the soft patter of rain on an umbrella, and don't mind getting wet themselves, but can't bear to see a child shivering in the rain.
17564: As a youngster they apprenticed on the abacus at a money house, with an excellent memory. When silver went missing from the vault, they found the altered figures by checking six months of ledgers in a row. They no longer manage money for the rich but still like sorting supplies into categories, make lists before setting out, and always ask for clarity on vague promises.
17565: They once ran a ferry and knew when each regular went home. One night a levee broke upstream, and they made more than ten trips back and forth to rescue trapped villagers, stopping only when the boat began to leak. They still wake with a start at the sound of rushing water, like drying nets on the bow, and never charge a fare to someone truly in trouble.
17566: As a child they helped support the family by making river lanterns, and know how to make thin paper float farther on the water. During a lantern festival they spotted a child who'd fallen in and found them by following the drifting lanterns. They like warm light that doesn't glare, and at festivals they quietly float a blank lantern in memory of those who never made it home.
17567: They once made rubbings of ancient steles for a stonemason, traveling for years between ruined temples and cliffs. Sheltering from the rain once, they noticed a crack in the rock wall and woke their companions in time to escape a collapse. They love collecting fragments of old characters and old paper, only look at ancient sites and never carve them, and are deeply angered by careless damage to what earlier generations left behind.
17568: From a family of plasterers and bricklayers, they learned to mix mud, build stoves and patch roofs as a child. In the rainy season they checked every house for unsafe walls and talked an old man who wouldn't leave into getting out. They can't sit still when they see a leak, love the smell of fresh mud drying, and believe houses, like hearts, need mending in time.
17569: In their youth they wrote letters for villagers who couldn't write, hearing many longings too painful to speak aloud. During the war they risked their life to save a chest of unsent letters home and sought out the recipients one by one. They're careful with their words, never reveal anyone's private affairs, like picking sturdy envelopes, and always keep a spare sheet of paper for travelers.
17570: They grew up in a hillside orchard and know grafting, pruning and judging when fruit is ripe. The year of the insect plague, they tried drawing birds into the orchard and saved the last few old trees. They love sweet-and-sour dried fruit and birdsong, notice whether trees could grow whenever they pass wasteland, and at harvest always share the best basket with the neighbors first.
17571: They once dried salt and fished in a bay, their skin roughened by sun and sea wind. Before a typhoon they noticed seabirds flying strangely low and went door to door urging the fishing boats back to port. They put great faith in nature's signs, like salty rations and wide-brimmed bamboo hats, and patiently talk people out of putting to sea just to prove themselves.
17572: As a youngster they made charcoal at a kiln and know the colors of smoke and the kiln's heat. Once, when the kiln mouth backfired, they pushed a younger apprentice clear and damaged their own voice in the smoke. Since then they say little but work meticulously, love mountain mist at dawn and the smell of pine, and always make sure there's ventilation before lighting a fire.
17573: They once kept a stall with a wandering incense and herb seller and learned to repel insects and calm nerves with flower water and herbs. When a fight broke out at a market, they lit reviving incense and guided the frightened crowd out of a narrow alley. They like clean clothes and subtle scents, often make small sachets for companions, but can't stand overpowering incense.
17574: As a child they copied sutras outside a temple in exchange for food; their handwriting is neat, though they don't understand much of the scripture. When bandits raided, they hid the temple's register in a woodpile and saved the land deeds the villagers had left there. They like quietly copying calligraphy and write out short lines when they're upset, and think little of people who use learning to lord it over others.
17575: Their family dealt in leather, and they learned to tan hides, sew boots and mend wrist guards as a child. One harsh winter, when a caravan lacked warm gear, they took apart their stock of leather goods overnight and made gloves for everyone. They care a lot about whether shoes and socks fit, like sturdy, hard-wearing things, and often fix companions' frayed straps.
17576: They were once an apprentice at a small-town hairdresser's and grew used to customers pouring out their troubles to the mirror. When a manhunt disturbed the neighborhood, they helped the constables identify the suspect by remembering his topknot. They're good at tidying clothes and hats and like wooden combs and fragrant hair oil, but never turn private things they've overheard into gossip.
17577: As a youngster they pounded soot and glue at an ink workshop, their hands always stained black. When the storeroom got damp, they caught the problem by smell and dried the whole batch of ink sticks overnight. They prefer drawings in crisp black and white, love the slow sound of grinding ink, and always like to finish the preparation before starting anything.
17578: They once guarded a village's forest and know every bird and animal call and the marks left by illegal logging. In the dry season they found embers reigniting and beat a gong alone to rally people to put out the forest fire. They always check the fire whenever they pass a camp, love planting trees and the sound of wind in the pines, and talk seriously to anyone who wastes wood.
17579: In their early years they patrolled a city ward at night, carrying a lamp down countless empty streets. Once they heard the faintest rattle of tiles and caught a thief breaking into an apothecary, without harming the coerced youngster with him. They sleep lightly, love the first bowl of soy milk in the morning, and always give someone who's done wrong a chance to explain.
17580: They shaved arrow shafts and glued feathers at a bow workshop and are unusually sensitive to how wood grain bends. Before a competition they found hidden cracks in a batch of shafts and, despite being scolded, insisted on replacing them, preventing an accident. They check their tools before doing anything, like collecting beautiful feathers, and disapprove of shooting for distance at the expense of accuracy.
17581: As a child they followed herders from pasture to pasture and can judge how far off grazing land is from cloud shadows. When wolves attacked at night, they lit damp grass to make thick smoke and protected the flock and the young ones. They love salty milk tea and the sound of wind through grass, and find it hard to stand by when the weak are ganged up on.
17582: They once escorted a famine relief grain convoy and saw with their own eyes that one sack of grain can save a family. When the steward tried to skim off "losses" on the way, they secretly recorded every weighing and exposed him in front of everyone. They share out supplies with strict fairness, like cutting rations into equal portions, and can't stand queue-jumping or hoarding public goods.
17583: Their hometown lacked water, and as a youngster they followed well diggers searching for underground springs. After months of digging they finally struck clear water on a barren slope and hurt their back in the process. They taste good water with care, like repairing well platforms and clearing ditches, and think hard work that benefits everyone is the most worthwhile kind.
17584: They once waited tables at an inn on the official road and could remember the orders of a dozen tables at once. In a drunken brawl they hid the children first, then stopped the fire from spreading with a basin of cold water. They're warm with people but don't fall for bragging, like hearing travelers talk about road conditions, and always notice who hasn't eaten enough.
17585: They once learned woodblock carving at a bookshop, where one wrong stroke means starting over. When war reached the city, they hid the blocks for common medical books in a cellar and later printed them again for village doctors. They're patient, like reading characters backwards and the smell of fresh ink on new books, and are happy to teach what they've learned to those who come after.
17586: As a youngster they carried a peddler's pole from village to village, selling everything from needles and thread to sweets. After a rockfall on a mountain road, they made a stretcher from their carrying pole and cloth and got an injured traveler to town. They like collecting little things from everywhere, haggle with a sense of proportion, and now and then deliberately undercharge a child with no money.
17587: They once tended the lamp of a lighthouse on a cape, climbing the long ladder every night to add oil and polish the mirror. Hearing a distress horn in thick fog, they rang the bell over and over to guide a lost ship. They dread a lamp going out for no reason, love the open sea and sturdy bronze mirrors, and never doze off on night watch.
17588: As a child they learned conjuring from street performers and are good at hiding things, slipping ropes and drawing the eye. In a market stampede they used colored flags to draw the crowd away and clear a path for the injured. They love making children laugh but would never count cheating the poor as a skill, and they despise real theft.
17589: Their family ran a mill, and they fell asleep to the sound of the millstone as a child. When floodwater poured into the mill, they risked opening the sluice and saved the nearby granary. They love the smell of freshly milled flour, like to work slowly and evenly, and when they're agitated they turn a small hand mill to calm down.
17590: In their early years they were a sailor on an ocean-going ship and learned to mend sails, read the wind and tie knots that hold. Once, when the mast snapped, they climbed the swaying rigging and cut away the torn sail to save the hull. They like wide views and sour dried fruit, stay especially calm in rough seas, but don't like talking about the loneliness of long voyages.
17591: They once helped in a temple's vegetarian kitchen and grew used to washing rice and chopping vegetables before dawn. When refugees fled up the mountain, they stretched the limited grain into thick porridge for seven days. They prefer simple vegetarian food, don't like others wasting the heat while cooking, and quietly remember who eats more and who eats less.
17592: When floodwater destroyed the village road, they led people in bamboo rafts back and forth between rooftops on rescues. On the last trip they brought back only a wooden chest holding a family genealogy, but it kept an old man's memories whole. They like wrapping important things against water, check low-lying spots when they hear heavy rain, and never laugh at anyone for treasuring old things.
17593: They grew up beside cotton fields and as a child picked and dried cotton. When a cold snap hit without warning, they led the villagers in harvesting overnight and saved the crop that would buy next year's grain. They love soft cotton cloth and sun-dried bedding, often restuff clothes with old cotton, and hate seeing anything still usable thrown away.
17594: Their family raised silkworms and reeled silk, and they're very sensitive to temperature and how fresh the mulberry leaves are. When disease hit the silkworm house, they decisively separated the sick trays and saved the season's work. They're careful in everything, like quietly watching for small changes, and though their clothes aren't fine, they look after every thread.
17595: As a youngster they boiled cane juice at a sugar mill and know that a little too much heat turns it burnt and bitter. Once, when a boiler cracked, they shut off the fire first and then got the workers out, scalding themselves on the steam. They love sweets but always give them away, think back on old times at the smell of caramel, and have more patience than most for waiting while things slowly take shape.
17596: They once sorted gears for a clockmaker in the city and can hear the faintest catch in a movement. When their master fell seriously ill, they repaired the great time-telling clock alone so the city didn't miss the hour to open the sluices. They're punctual to the point of stubbornness and like taking small mechanisms apart, but will hear out someone who's late if there's a real reason.
17597: They spent years traveling mountain roads with mule trains and know the animals' tempers and how to tie down cargo. When a cliff path collapsed, they unloaded the valuable chests themselves so people and animals could cross lightly first. They believe lives matter more than cargo, like strong tea, thick blankets and unhurried mounts, and disapprove of pushing tired companions on.
17598: As a youngster they lived at a boxing school and could only earn the right to watch by sweeping floors and carrying water. When a senior got hurt sparring, they pointed out the faulty use of force from what they'd observed, and were formally taken in. They train diligently, like sweeping the training ground, take the basics especially seriously, and are happy to train newcomers starting from the simplest move.
17599: They once lived beside a salt lake on the plateau and judged the seasons by watching migrating birds. Before a blizzard the flocks suddenly flew south, and they moved the herders to a sheltered valley in time. They like identifying feathers and clouds, often look up at the sky as they walk, and strongly dislike killing birds returning to their nests.
17600: In their early years they painted temple murals, only mixing colors and outlining, but secretly practiced drawing faces and expressions for years. After a fire, they repainted the lost murals from memory. They love collecting mineral pigments, pay particular attention to people's eyes, and stop to memorize the shifting colors of a beautiful view.
17601: They once drummed in a festival drum troupe and know how to keep a crowd's steps in time with rhythm. When the city gate caught fire, they kept drumming to guide the evacuation until the drumhead was soaked through with rain. They tap out a beat without thinking when they hear ragged footsteps, love bustle but not crowds, and are very good at lifting tired companions' spirits.
17602: Their family ran a fireworks workshop, and they were taught from childhood that carelessness is gunpowder's greatest danger. When an apprentice broke the rules by bringing a lamp into the store, they snatched the flame away in time and averted disaster. They take safety rules very seriously, love festive night skies but never get too close, and always store dangerous materials separately whatever they're making.
17603: In their youth they helped at a tavern and saw countless quarrels start over a cup of wine. They once cleared up a years-long misunderstanding between two families with old accounts and witnesses, preventing a brawl. They're good at letting people finish what they're saying, like peanuts and light wine, and if both sides are seething, they quietly move any weapons out of reach first.
17604: They grew up at the foot of the snowy mountains, joining their elders' winter hunts to stock the village's food. Once, lost in a blizzard, they led the whole party back by the branches they'd broken along the way. They always pack two sets of fire-starting gear before going into the mountains, love thick fur hats and the smell of pine resin, and sternly warn anyone who takes risks without preparing.
17605: They once made a living carrying loads on a pole, climbing dozens of li of stone steps a day. When a mountain path gave way, they dropped all the goods and used the carrying pole to pull up a child hanging over the edge. Their shoulders are thickly calloused. They like flat paths and sturdy straw sandals, and when they meet someone carrying too much, they always take the load for a stretch.
17606: As a youngster they weeded and watered an herb garden and can tell seedlings from weeds by the finest differences. During an insect plague they tried interplanting pest-repelling herbs and saved several patches of precious medicinal seedlings. They love the smell of soil and dried herb leaves, observe patiently before deciding, and don't write off unfamiliar things as useless.
17607: They once polished bronze mirrors in a mirror maker's shop and know even the finest scratch spoils the reflection. When a rich family pressured their master into passing off shoddy work, they exposed it publicly and left. They dress neatly but not lavishly, like polishing old objects, and believe seeing your own faults clearly matters more than hearing flattery.
17608: Their family made ropes and nets for a living, and they could tie a dozen knots blindfolded as a child. During a flood rescue they linked rooftops with long ropes so dozens of people could cross one by one. They always carry a small coil of hemp rope, like tying loose things up neatly, and care a great deal whether companions look out for each other.
17609: Their hometown had only one mountain spring, and as a youngster they took turns clearing its source. They once found someone dumping filth upstream, tracked them down alone and persuaded every village to agree on rules to protect the water. They check where water comes from before drinking, love the sound of a cool spring, and will take on seemingly petty responsibilities for things everyone shares.
17610: In their early years they helped maintain the official road, planting trees, filling potholes and setting up milestones. When heavy rain washed away the road markers, they put them back up overnight so caravans wouldn't stray into a dangerous valley. They move stones off the path as they walk, love shade trees and straight roads, and believe making things easier for those who come later is a virtue too.
17611: During the war they escorted a group of lost children to a safe town, keeping their fear at bay with stories all the way. After arriving, they spent months finding each child's family. They're especially patient with children and always carry sweets, but won't stand for anyone shaming others for an orphan's background.
17612: After a disaster they kept the register of names and origins at a temporary camp and found that many separated families were only an accurate list away from each other. They stayed up night after night sorting clues and finally reunited dozens of households. They're excellent at remembering names, like tidy records, and double-check every entry however busy they are.
17613: They once went into the snowy mountains with a quarrying team looking for crystal ore and were trapped in an ice cave for two days after an avalanche. By tapping on the rock wall they got an answer from outside and kept the wounded alive until rescue came. They fear sudden loud noises but love the colors of light through crystal, and always rope themselves to their companions in the mountains.
17614: In their youth they pulled an oar on a navy ship and know flag signals and tides. When the flagship lost its way in a night battle, they read the waterway from faint lights on shore and steered clear of hidden stakes. They've left the army but still keep their things as neat as a ship's cabin. They follow orders, but always check first that no innocents will be hurt.
17615: From a family of tile makers, they know clay, kiln heat and the sound of a struck tile. After an earthquake they led the villagers in patching the schoolhouse with intact old tiles so the children could go back before the rainy season. They love the sound of rain dripping from the eaves, climb a ladder to fix any loose tile they see, and like everything to be fully covered.
17616: They once weighed cargo at the docks, strong but trusting the steelyard more. When they found the steward had secretly altered the weights to cheat the boatmen, they exposed it publicly by checking against a standard stone. They care a great deal about fairness in trade and like calibrating tools, but if someone admits their mistake and makes it right, they let it go.
17617: As a youngster they surveyed post roads with craftsmen, measuring slopes, noting water sources and clearing dangerous rocks. With mountain rain coming, they insisted the team stop work and avoided a mudslide. They always study the terrain before setting out, like marking wells on maps, and are wary of decisions that chase shortcuts and ignore the risks.
17618: They once drew rough maps for traveling merchants, correcting directions by paces, the sun's shadow and landmarks. Finding that an old map put a village beside a dangerous swamp, they walked the route again themselves to correct it. They love climbing high to look into the distance, leave clear marks at every fork, and are happy to hear locals describe the real state of the roads.
17619: As a child they helped a puppet troupe pull strings and change scenery and know mechanisms and the rhythm of the stage. When the show tent collapsed, they crawled behind the curtain and rescued trapped performers. They like carving puppet faces and watch people's hands closely. They hate the feeling of someone pulling the strings of their fate and deeply respect those who dare make their own choices.
17620: They once looked after rare birds for a rich family but preferred ordinary tits. When the aviary caught fire, they opened every cage and let the birds go, and lost their job for it. They carry a little grain with them, love birdsong at dawn, go quiet for a long time when they see a cage that's too small, and would never trade freedom for security.
17621: They've drifted through the jianghu for years as a day laborer, guard and guide, and at their lowest received a meal from strangers in a village. Since then, wherever they go, they help mend roads and carry water unasked. They like remembering the kindnesses they've met along the way, own nothing of value, yet always keep a little spare food for whoever needs it.
17622: As a girl she learned pattern drawing and color matching at an embroidery workshop. When the storeroom caught fire, she led the women in wrapping the precious embroidery designs in wet cloth and saved years of work from the thick smoke. She carries needle, thread and small scissors, likes studying the patterns of flowers and leaves, quietly mends any torn hem, and is happy to teach young girls the most basic stitches.
17623: As a child she followed her mother delivering babies for the neighbors and knows boiling water, preparing cloth and comforting mothers in labor. The night a flash flood closed the road, she went out alone in the rain to fetch a doctor and watched over a mother and daughter until dawn. She's steady in a crisis, always keeps clean soft cloth in her pack, and can't stand anyone joking about the hardship of childbirth.
17624: As a girl she rode escorts with her father and brothers. Because people always looked down on her, she memorized routes, code signs and horses' tempers better than anyone. In a night ambush she posed as an ordinary woman of the household to lure the bandits away so injured companions could get the cargo to safety. She doesn't like boasting of her skills, but always checks the axles and knots herself before setting out.
17625: She grew up in an opera troupe playing the young female lead, training in water sleeves, stage movement and high leaps. When the star fell ill, she stepped in and held a full house, then after the show led the younger girls away from thugs who'd come to make trouble. She likes collecting old opera lines and adjusts her step without thinking at the sound of gongs and drums, but doesn't want anyone to judge her skill by her makeup alone.
17626: She was once the only woman storyteller at a teahouse, at first only allowed to fill in her master's lines from behind a curtain. When heavy snow sealed the city, she told stories for days on end to calm stranded travelers and turned her tips into charcoal for everyone. She speaks clearly, likes recording tales from all over, and patiently corrects the old stories that give heroines' deeds to someone else.
17627: A girl who grew up in a weaving workshop, she's alert to the faintest odd noise among the looms. She once noticed a loose crossbeam and stopped a whole row of looms in time, saving the women working overtime. She's good at fixing small mechanisms, likes keeping spools in neat rows, and with any complicated problem, she first looks for the thread that came loose first.
17628: In her youth she was a woman constable, often sent to question witnesses who wouldn't talk to men because she was so thorough. She once followed the trail from an unremarkable hairpin to a child-trafficking ring and rescued three missing girls overnight. She still habitually checks doors, windows and footprints, and her voice turns especially hard with bullies.
17629: Born to a boat family on the river and called the boat girl from childhood, she can hold the helm steady in rapids. One stormy night she rowed a small boat through a rocky shoal to get a woman in labor to a clinic on shore. She loves open water and sun-dried mooring ropes, checks the wind before boarding, and always saves an inside seat for companions who are afraid of water.
17630: She once taught girls to read and keep accounts at a village girls' school; most of her students worked by day and came to class at night. During the fighting she hid the register and textbooks in a grain jar and afterwards went door to door to find her scattered students. She carries a short pencil, likes breaking hard characters apart to explain them, and believes learning to write your own name is the first step to taking charge of your fate.
17631: As a girl she learned the herbs women commonly use from a village medicine woman and often recorded symptoms for patients too shy to speak. During an epidemic she insisted on boiling the sick's drinking water separately and led several women in taking shifts to care for a whole lane. She can smell whether herbs have gone damp. She's gentle with people but will never tolerate folk remedies that cost lives.
17632: Her family ran a small winery, and in her youth she trod the yeast, sealed jars and recorded the bottling dates. When the steward tried to sell spoiled wine to outsiders, she smashed the bad jars in front of everyone and was thrown out of the shop for it. She only drinks light wine now, likes telling grains apart by their aroma, and a cup she promises someone is never watered down.
17633: As a child she learned color mixing from the women at a dye works, her hands always stained a faint blue that won't wash off. When the river rose, she led the women in moving the dyes up onto high racks so they wouldn't poison the wells downstream. She loves the colors of cloth drying on a sunny day, is very sparing with any dye, and cleans up any ditch she's stained without being asked.
17634: As a girl she hunted in the mountains with her aunt and is good at setting snares that trap without hurting. One harsh winter she followed tracks to find a girl lost gathering firewood and carried her back to the village wrapped in her cloak. She holds the mountain forests in awe, likes sharpening her small knife and collecting feathers, and only draws her bow when she truly has to.
17635: She once led the dancers in a festival troupe and is highly practiced with long silk ribbons and drumbeats. When a stampede broke out in the city, she climbed onto a platform and waved colored silk to split the crowd, getting her young juniors safely to open ground. She loves festive lights but always notes the exits first, and when she sees a crush she reminds people to slow down.
17636: In her youth she kept the accounts for a caravan, never once wrong on the abacus or the cargo lists. On the road she found the steward skimming the women workers' pay, quietly kept a copy of every handover, and eventually won back what they were owed. She cares especially about receipts in trade, likes keeping small change in separate pouches, and is happy to teach girls who can't count to check their wages.
17637: She was once a woman archer in a frontier town, passing flag signals between beacon towers. When enemies attacked under thick fog that hid the walls, she judged their approach by the sound of the wind and cut three scaling ropes in a row, buying time for reinforcements. She doesn't like talking about her service, still habitually sits with her back to a wall, and is always the first to notice when a bowstring is getting damp.
17638: Her family has raised silkworms for generations, and as a girl she could tell from the smell of mulberry leaves whether they'd suit the worms. The year disease struck the silkworm house, she separated the sick trays despite her elders' objections and led the other girls in saving the last healthy worms. She's meticulous, likes soft lamplight and fresh mulberry leaves, and often reminds companions that small changes are usually the ones most worth noticing.
17639: She was once an apprentice at a mechanism shop, at first only allowed to sweep and hand over tools. After her master was hurt, she fixed the city gate's jammed winch alone so the grain carts could get through in time. She likes taking apart old locks and worn gears, rarely argues when doubted, and simply puts the repaired mechanism firmly back in place.
17640: As a girl she carried letters along the post road and knows every bridge and every cave to shelter from rain along the way. When a landslide blocked a mountain road, she took a two-day detour to get military intelligence to the pass, and on the way back brought a stranded mother and daughter with her. She treasures light boots and an oilcloth mailbag, and delivers every message she takes on word for word, however long or short.

19787: Most of Jingyun Mountain's disciples are women. They revere harmony with nature, excel with swords and sabers, and defend rather than attack.
19788: Longhu Palace is a traditional Daoist sect devoted to cultivating the true self. It excels at fist arts, is well-rounded, and balances hard and soft.
19789: Every Tieqi Sect disciple is tall and powerfully built. They prize tempering the body, with moves in a supporting role; their martial arts are all about attack!
19790: The Jueying Sect is an assassins' sect that runs most of the assassination business under heaven, but what they love most is actually studying art.
19791: Yinsha Manor is a gathering of fanatics who research life. They worship the cycle of life and death and are determined to prove their theories, whatever the world thinks.
19792: Far off on Kunlun, the immortal mountain of the Western Regions, away from the Central Plains' conflicts, it has a lofty air all its own. Its Three Saints of Qin, Go and Sword once held sway over the region. Its martial style is bold and sweeping, with the wildness of the Western Regions yet true to orthodox Daoist mystic arts. Being so remote, it holds countless rare treasures, but its members tend to be proud and extreme, often drawing swords at the first disagreement.
19793: Hidden in drifting clouds and mist, it admits only those of peerless beauty and talent. The sect's learning is vast: medicine, divination, astrology, physiognomy, qin, go, calligraphy and painting, it masters them all. Its martial arts are beyond belief: it can absorb others' power for its own use and even turn back the years. Xiaoyao disciples do as they please, neither clearly righteous nor evil, the most mysterious and refined hidden sect in the jianghu.
19794: I'm sure you can manage your disciples well now. Please take on the challenges ahead; I believe you'll lead your disciples to glory step by step. This demo only opens part of the content, but more challenges and content are coming. If you enjoyed it, please add the game to your wishlist; that's the greatest motivation for us! We look forward to seeing you in the full release. For now, please carry on with your game.
19795: When my father pressed this seal into my hand, his palm was hotter than this fire. All he said was "Protect the sect", yet now all I can do is lead everyone into hiding in this valley.
19796: Young Master, you mustn't sell yourself short! We'll take back Wangyue Peak!
19797: We await your orders, Young Master!
19798: Rest well tonight; from tomorrow we work in groups. Those badly hurt, study the heart method to regulate your inner breath. The lightly wounded, come with me to clear land. You, take the rest and build defenses. We have to put down roots in this wilderness first.
19799: Young Master, there may be wild beasts about at night. Shall a disciple keep watch?
19800: No need. This place looks safe enough to me, and with the fire going, beasts won't dare attack.
19801: Sect Master, we've rested well and await your orders!
19802: Do you still remember the night view from Wangyue Peak?
19803: I remember, Sect Master! At full moon the moonlight flowed down the white jade steps like a layer of silver frost.
19804: And the Qingyun Hall on the main peak, whose twelve coiling-dragon pillars glowed at night. Father said it was the guardian power the founder left to protect the hall.
19805: Our Qingyun Sect guarded the southwest for three hundred years, keeping the eighteen towns below the mountain safe from bandits. Father always said true martial arts aren't for fighting but for protecting.
19806: But the jianghu doesn't always listen to reason. Those men in black destroyed our sect because they were afraid we'd stand in their way.
19808: The Xueying Order. Ten years ago they were just a small sect, but now they dare covet the martial arts canons of every great sect. Father died protecting the last three volumes of the Qingyun Heart Sutra...
19809: [Rises in anger] Once we've recovered our strength, we'll make them pay in blood!
19810: Revenge can wait. The jianghu is vast: besides the Xueying Order, there's the Tieqi Alliance in the north and Penglai Pavilion in the East Sea, all eyeing the land of fallen sects like ours. What we need to do now is survive, and grow stronger than anyone.
19811: Sect Master, will we ever get back to Wangyue Peak?
19812: As long as this fire doesn't go out, as long as Qingyun lives in our hearts, the day will come when we return. And when it does, we won't just rebuild the sect, we'll make the name of the Qingyun Sect ring through the jianghu again!
19813: Tonight's stars look just like the star chart over Wangyue Peak.
19814: They do. The stars always show the way home.
19815: Sect Master, I've hung the wooden board carved with the daily schedule in the most visible spot, so everyone can see the routine.
19816: Thank you for your concern, Sect Master. It's just... my skills aren't good enough, and a bandit gave me a cut. It's nothing serious.
19817: Sect Master, someone from down the mountain has come to see you!
19819: It stretches deep into the endless forest, wrapped in blue mist all year. Villagers sometimes go in to hunt and gather lingzhi, and now and then see traces of strange beasts.
19820: Rumored in the jianghu to be a gathering place for villains. The valley mouth is full of thorn traps, dark clouds never leave the valley, and screams sometimes ring out, chilling anyone passing by.
